Industry News: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A Fresh Frontier and Use Cases

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • Recent findings suggest that every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Recent findings suggest that every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to latest series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Sources indicate that figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

Recent findings suggest that now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

It has been revealed that the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

Recent findings suggest that businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

Recent findings suggest that -Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

Industry observers note that -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

Industry observers note that -Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

It has been revealed that an ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a newly introduced cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

Industry observers note that to get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Sources indicate that figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

In a recent development, A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each upcoming reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

Sources indicate that with AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

According to recent reports, figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Industry observers note that fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

According to recent reports, if a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

According to recent reports, TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

It has been revealed that this application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

Recent findings suggest that figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

#3375. Latest Update: RACE: Ranking-Uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (208 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: RACE: Ranking-Uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.18244v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity. A lightweight predictor is then trained via self-supervision to anticipate this uncertainty from early-layer features. Guided by this signal, RACE performs instance-specific slimming in two dimensions: a hypernetwork-style channel sensitivity extractor identifies parameter redundancy, while importance-aware progressive sequence filtering mitigates data redundancy. Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate that RACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.

This could allow an attacker who can manipulate the ticket response to write arbitrary files outside the intended download directory and, when overwriting is enabled, replace existing files accessible to the application. #3372. Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard

Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy rapidly.
  • In a recent development, today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard, a fresh way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio.
  • The leaderboard is a newly introduced view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy rapidly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case.

In a recent development, today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard, a fresh way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model.

The leaderboard is a newly introduced view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it demonstrates two kinds of information:.

Recent findings suggest that because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers 70+ models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time.

The following screenshot highlights the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model.

Figure 1: Leaderboard overview in SageMaker Studio.

This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves.

A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs:.

Higher is better for all three. The leaderboard highlights each benchmark separately rather than blending them into one number. That keeps the results transparent: You can weigh the benchmarks that matter for your application and check each score against the public definition of the benchmark.

Sources indicate that speed and cost depend on your workload and on how the model is deployed. Two menus above the leaderboard control which performance and cost numbers you see:.

Each optimization goal picks a different configuration:.

In a recent development, A note on cost: Estimated cost reflects SageMaker instance cost only, based on the on-demand hourly rate for the configuration’s default instance type. It does not include data transfer, storage, inference component costs, or discounts such as Reserved Instances or AWS Savings Plans. Your actual bill will vary. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator for billing estimates.

Published benchmark scores often come from different teams using different prompts, settings, and hardware, which makes them hard to compare. We took a different approach:.

For full details, including prompts, generation settings, and how configurations are measured, see JumpStart leaderboard methodology.

The following steps show how to go from browsing to a deployed model. You need access to SageMaker Studio and permission to deploy JumpStart models.

In SageMaker Studio, open the Models page, then select the Leaderboard view. The leaderboard keeps the same search bar and filters as the other views, and it has its own URL. You can bookmark it or share a direct link with your team.

The following screenshot demonstrates the Models page with the Leaderboard view selected.

Figure 2: JumpStart base models page with the Leaderboard view selected.

Use the same search and filters you already use elsewhere in JumpStart to keep only the models that fit your requirements. Common filters include license, provider, and input and output modality. Start with hard requirements, for example a license that allows commercial use, before you look at scores.

The following screenshot indicates the leaderboard filtered by input modality, output modality, and license.

Figure 3: Leaderboard with filters applied.

Industry observers note that above the leaderboard, select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu (default: Max Context). Then choose a goal from the Optimized for menu (default: Balanced). For a chatbot your customers interact with, Latency optimized is a sensible start. For overnight document processing, Throughput optimized or Cost optimized may fit better. The performance and cost columns patch, and quality scores stay the same.

The following screenshots show the View benchmarks for your use case and Optimized for menus above the leaderboard.

Figure 4: View benchmarks for your use case menu.

In a recent development, each column has a blue heatmap, so the top-performing models stand out at a glance: the deeper the blue, the stronger the result in that column. Sort any benchmark column to rank models by the metric you care about most. Use the column settings (gear icon) to hide metrics you don’t need, and scroll horizontally to see more. The model name columns stay frozen as you scroll, and a fade at the edge demonstrates when more columns are available.

The following screenshot highlights the heatmap and the column settings menu.

Figure 6: Heatmap and column settings.

Choose a model to open it. From there, you have options to deploy the model or, for models that support serverless customization, to customize it. If you deploy, choose the same use case and optimization goal you compared on the leaderboard. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on, and a different configuration can change quality, latency, throughput, and cost.

The following screenshot demonstrates a model page with the Deploy and Customize options.

Figure 7: Model page with the Deploy and Customize options.

Suppose you are building an internal help-desk assistant. Employees ask questions and expect fast, accurate answers that follow a set response format. You need a commercially licensed model and want to keep costs predictable.

After filtering by license and choosing a chat-like use case profile with Latency optimized, your shortlist might look like this:.

In a recent development, reading the table, Model A has the highest knowledge score but also the highest cost and the slowest first response. Model B scores almost as well, holds up on multi-step reasoning, and runs on a smaller, cheaper instance. For a help desk, where reasoning through a question and responding promptly matter more than the last few points of general knowledge, Model B is the better starting point. A bigger model is not always the better choice, and the leaderboard makes that trade-off visible in seconds.

From there, you would deploy Model B, test it with real questions from your help desk, and keep Model C in mind as a lower-cost option if quality holds up.

We’re continuing to expand the leaderboard. Areas we’re exploring include:.

It has been revealed that the SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard brings quality, speed, and cost together in one place, measured consistently on SageMaker. Instead of comparing numbers from different sources, you can filter to the models that fit your requirements, compare them on the configuration you proposal to run, and deploy with a few clicks.

Recent findings suggest that to get started, open the Models page in SageMaker Studio and select the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see the following resources:.

Open the leaderboard, shortlist two or three models for your workload, and deploy them to test with your own prompts before you choose one for production.

#3370. EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (212 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (212 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.16728v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that shares manipulation structure through fine-grained, semantically corresponding observation and action modalities while keeping sensing and control interfaces embodiment-specific. EgoX pretrains a Modular Embodiment Dreamer (MED) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MED assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MED's average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.

#3367. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1398 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That proposal is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

In a recent development, better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It notes nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

Sources indicate that the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

According to recent reports, for a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

Industry observers note that this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

Sources indicate that these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

Industry observers note that we treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

Industry observers note that we compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

Industry observers note that A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It reveals how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

In a recent development, linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

According to recent reports, catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Sources indicate that feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

It has been revealed that one caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

Industry observers note that up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Sources indicate that out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

Industry observers note that more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

Recent findings suggest that view CSAF Summary Mendix Studio Pro contains multiple vulnerabilities in the MCP Server, that could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the server remotely or trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests, potentially leading to unauthorized data access, tool execution, or system compromise. Siemens has released newly introduced versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. The following versions of Siemens Mendix Studio Pro are affected: Mendix Studio Pro 11 vers:intdot/>=11.15.0|<11.16.0 (CVE-2026-112136, CVE-2026-112137) Mendix Studio Pro 11.12 vers:intdot/>=11.12.6|<11.12.7 (CVE-2026-112136, CVE-2026-112137) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Siemens Mendix Studio Pro 11 2 Vulnerabilities Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Manufacturer Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-112136 The affected products MCP Server does not properly restrict its HTTP listener to the loopback interface, leaving it potentially exposed to remote systems. This could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the MCP Server remotely. Read More 2 Affected Products Mendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations MitigationMaintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to upgrade to the latest versions.

Breaking: Spec-Driven PBT: Deriving Semantic Invariants from Code Specifications for Agentic Property-based Testing

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (294 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.15920v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Software is increasingly written by AI agents that produce an implementation from a natural language specification, a practice known as agentic coding. Code is now produced faster than it can be reviewed, and has been shown to exhibit its own characteristic failure patterns. Property-based testing (PBT), a long-standing technique in which invariant properties of a program are checked against many generated inputs, has recently been revisited with LLM agents authoring the properties, thereby removing the high-effort derivation of invariants that has long hindered its adoption. Existing methods, however, derive these properties from the implementation alone (Code-driven PBT). At the same time, a thorough specification such as a product requirements document has become routine within agentic coding, yet its role in testing the resulting code remains underexplored. We study the value of the specification as a source of properties for testing agent-written code. Our key insight is that the specification, unlike the implementation, records what the code was meant to do, and invariants derived from it are not biased by particular implementation choices. We propose Spec-Driven PBT, an agent that first expresses invariants in natural language from the specification and only then inspects the implementation to translate them into concrete tests. Across 25 applications from ViBench, Spec-Driven PBT finds a novel set of bugs that Code-driven PBT misses, while writing 2.4x fewer property tests. Though the two approaches surface a roughly equivalent number of bugs, there is little overlap: nearly 60% of the 169 total bugs are found by only one. Qualitatively, we find that the bugs unique to Spec-Driven PBT tend to violate documented product workflows whereas those to Code-driven PBT instead concentrate on implementation robustness, offering complementary value for bug discovery in agent-written code.

View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to retrieve sensitive system information, access application data without authorization, recover stored credentials, or intercept and manipulate network communications. The following versions of Dorsett Controls InfoScan are affected: InfoScan <=1.45.0 (CVE-2026-117659, CVE-2026-120157, CVE-2026-120255, CVE-2026-120260, CVE-2026-120271, CVE-2026-120298) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.1 Dorsett Controls InfoScan 5 Vulnerabilities Improper Certificate Validation, Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere, Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key, Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Manufacturer Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-117659 The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection. Read More 1 Affected Product Dorsett Controls InfoScan <=1.45.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixDorsett Controls recommends updating affected versions of InfoScan to v1.46 or higher. To install the security patch, user administrators will need to log in to InfoScan and select System Maintenance from the menu. Once the System Maintenance application is open, select Check for Updates, and click the Install Now button in the Ready To Install section. If you are an offline customer (InfoScan has no internet access), you will need to download the patch from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal by selecting the InfoScan Update tile, downloading the update, and following the instructions listed on the portal. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3216 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy.
  • In a recent development, sageMaker HyperPod already handles nodes that report hardware faults.
  • In a recent development, in this post, we walk through the three upcoming capabilities that catch these failures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still demonstrates it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin. Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training. Today, we’re introducing workload recovery and infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod that catch these failures sooner and raise the goodput of your training workloads.

In a recent development, sageMaker HyperPod already handles nodes that report hardware faults. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware. These features look at one node’s hardware at a time. They can’t tell whether the GPUs train correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the Kubernetes components a job depends on are working.

In a recent development, in this post, we walk through the three upcoming capabilities that catch these failures. For each one, we show how to set it up and what it reports when it finds a problem:.

Industry observers note that the existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors. The InstanceStress deep health check runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices. The InstanceConnectivity check runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium. Together, these confirm that each node’s hardware works. They don’t show whether the GPUs compute correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the cluster’s Kubernetes components are healthy. Three kinds of failure get past them:.

It has been revealed that each capability covers a different point in a training run. MultiNodeTrainingValidation runs when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirms that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the cluster continuously and, when a job fails, reports the pods and nodes that were involved. The following table summarizes the three.

Hung job detection is upcoming for Slurm clusters. On EKS clusters, HyperPod already detects hung jobs that run through the HyperPod training operator, and Ray Train jobs get hang detection by default. We describe both options in the hung job detection section.

Each capability targets a different source of lost goodput. Scheduling goodput is the share of time that all the resources a job needs are available. Runtime goodput is the share of that time in which the job makes forward progress. Program goodput is the share of the hardware’s peak performance that the job gets. The following table highlights the effect of each capability.

Consider a pre-training job running on 32 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (256 NVIDIA H100 GPUs). If the job hangs at 1:00 AM and no one notices until 9:00 AM, it wastes 256 instance-hours or 2,048 GPU-hours. At the SageMaker HyperPod on-demand price of approximately $66 per instance-hour in US East (N. Virginia), the hang costs about $16,900. With a 15-minute hung job detection rule, HyperPod cancels the stalled job and Slurm requeues it. The hang costs about $530 instead, saving approximately $16,400.

According to recent reports, the MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check trains a fixed, known-good workload, first on each instance and then across instances. It catches GPUs that pass InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity but produce NaN or infinite loss once they train together. If an instance fails, HyperPod labels it as failed and, with automatic node recovery turned on, reboots or replaces it. When the check runs during provisioning, this happens before your jobs can use the instance.

MultiNodeTrainingValidation adds two tests to the deep health check run:.

Either test fails an instance if the training loss becomes NaN or infinite, or if training doesn’t finish within the time limit. The workload is fixed, so a failure points to the hardware rather than to a model or code change.

The following table shows how it fits with the other deep health checks.

Sources indicate that hyperPod runs deep health checks when it creates or updates instances. To include MultiNodeTrainingValidation, add it to OnStartDeepHealthChecks in the instance group configuration that you pass to create-cluster or patch-cluster. We turned on all three checks:.

To confirm the setting, run the following command:.

The output lists the three checks:.

Sources indicate that you can also check instances that are already in the cluster, for example before a long pre-training run. Use the StartClusterHealthCheck API:.

To check specific instances instead of the whole group, add "InstanceIds": [...] to the configuration.

Recent findings suggest that hyperPod writes one line per test to the DeepHealthCheckResults/ log stream in your cluster’s CloudWatch log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters//. Here’s the stream from our run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. TINY_MEGATRON and MEGATRON are the two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests:.

When the run finishes, each instance carries the result as a node label:.

For the training details, read /var/log/aws/clusters/sagemaker-deep-health-check.log on the instance, for example through an AWS Systems Manager session. On the instance that ran rank 0, the log ends with a summary of the Megatron test:.

The other instance’s log has a line for every iteration, with the loss and a running count of NaN iterations:.

In our run, the loss fell from 11.57 to 3.62 over 300 iterations, with no NaN or skipped iterations, at about 507 milliseconds per iteration on 16 H100 GPUs.

On our two-node cluster, the full deep health check took 1 hour 28 minutes after the instances finished their lifecycle scripts. DCGM level 4 diagnostics took most of that. The two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests added about 8 minutes. Instances can’t take workloads until the checks finish, so plan for this additional time when you add capacity.

In a recent development, keep in mind that MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests the hardware with a fixed reference workload. A pass means the instances trained that workload correctly. It doesn’t guarantee that your own job will converge. We recommend running it on fresh capacity, on replacement instances, and before long pre-training runs.

Industry observers note that HMA watches the hardware on each node, but many failures that stop a training job happen in Kubernetes. A device plugin can crash-loop until its node stops offering GPUs to the scheduler, or a taint can evict a job’s pods. The job error rarely names the pod or node involved, so engineers piece together what happened from kubectl output, per-rank logs, and timestamps.

The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches these resources from one place in the cluster. When something breaks, it tells you what changed and which nodes, pods, and jobs are affected. It reports through Kubernetes events and structured CloudWatch logs. The agent only reports. It doesn’t reboot nodes or restart jobs, because the cause might be in the workload. HMA and HyperPod node recovery still handle hardware faults, and the HyperPod training operator still handles job restarts.

The agent runs as a single pod per cluster in the aws-hyperpod namespace and prefers CPU nodes, so it doesn’t use GPU capacity. It watches the following:.

The agent reports what it finds in two places:.

The following table lists the events you’re most likely to see.

For the full list of events, see the documentation.

Industry observers note that if your cluster already uses the HyperPod Helm chart, apply the agent’s custom resource definition (CRD) first, because Helm doesn’t install CRDs during an upgrade. Then upgrade the release with the agent turned on:.

The upgrade also moves the other HyperPod components in the chart, such as HMA and the device plugins, to the chart’s current versions. To see what will change first, run the same command with --dry-run=server.

Check that the agent is running and that its health report exists:.

The health report lists the HyperPod components that the agent tracks, such as HMA, and when their status last changed:.

By default, HMA is the only required DaemonSet. If your cluster uses the device plugins from the HyperPod Helm chart, add them so that the agent reports a missing plugin. Also add the namespaces where your training jobs run, so that it can link pod failures to their jobs. Each list replaces its default, so keep the default entries. Save the following as krma-values.yaml:.

To see how the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent handles an infrastructure failure, we deployed a small DaemonSet into aws-hyperpod, pinned it to one node, and made it exit a few seconds after starting. It behaves like a crash-looping device plugin without touching the real one. Within seconds, the agent raised events on the pod and the DaemonSet:.

It has been revealed that next, we ran a two-node HyperPodPyTorchJob and made one rank exit during training. The agent raised a TrainingJobFailed event on the job:.

It also wrote the failure to CloudWatch with the pods and nodes involved, so you don’t need to look them up from the job’s pod list:.

The agent writes these logs to the cluster log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters//, in streams named SageMakerClusterMonitoringAgent//. It starts a newly introduced stream when it moves to another node, so filter by the stream prefix. For sample queries, see the documentation.

According to recent reports, NCCL 2.24 and later include the reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem, a small listener in each NCCL process that reports the state of the job’s communicators. For jobs that opt in, the agent reads this report from every pod every 30 seconds.

It has been revealed that by default, NCCL binds the RAS listener to localhost inside the pod, where the agent can’t reach it. To opt a job in, you bind the listener to the pod IP instead. That makes port 28028 reachable on the pod network, which NVIDIA’s documentation notes has security implications. Before you turn it on, apply a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that allows TCP port 28028 only from the agent’s pod and still allows traffic between the job’s own pods. The agent’s documentation includes an example policy. Then set NCCL_RAS_ADDR in the training container:.

To confirm the setting, turn on NCCL debug logging with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,RAS. Each rank then logs the address RAS listens on:.

If the address is ::1 or 127.0.0.1, NCCL_RAS_ADDR isn’t set and the agent can’t reach the listener.

Industry observers note that for each monitored job, the agent combines the per-pod results into a job-level state. The job is healthy when every pod returns a valid report, degraded when only some do, and unhealthy when none do. Unhealthy usually means the training processes have stopped.

Sources indicate that the agent logs a summary after each polling cycle. In a run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances, every cycle reported both training pods healthy, 30 seconds apart:.

The agent also writes each RAS report to CloudWatch, so you can spot communicator problems while the job is still running. In our test, we made one rank of a two-node job stop calling all_reduce. The report from the next polling cycle showed the communicator out of step and named the rank, GPU, process, and node that had fallen behind:.

Rank 1 is one operation behind rank 0, so start with rank 1’s GPU on node 10.0.2.22.

Industry observers note that A training job can hang without exiting. An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can leave the job holding its GPUs while Slurm still demonstrates it as running. It stays that way until someone notices that the loss or the log has stopped changing. Teams that run Slurm often build their own watchdog scripts and alarms to catch these jobs, and then need to maintain them.

According to recent reports, today, we’re launching hung job detection for SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters. It finds these jobs, writes an event to CloudWatch, and can cancel a hung job so that Slurm puts it back in the queue. You turn it on for each job with an environment variable that points to a small rules file. It needs no changes to your training scripts or containers, and it works with PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and custom scripts.

It has been revealed that hung job detection runs as an agent on every node and is off by default. The agent watches only jobs that set the HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES environment variable to the path of a rules file. The rules file decides how the agent detects a hang:.

When the agent declares a hang, it writes a HANG_DETECTED event to CloudWatch. If the rules file sets the action to cancel, the agent also cancels the job and Slurm requeues it. With the default action, notify, the agent writes the event and leaves the job running.

Hung job detection is separate from auto-resume, which restarts jobs that exit after a hardware failure. Auto-resume handles jobs that crash and hung job detection handles jobs that keep running without making progress.

On HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, HyperPod already detects hung jobs in two cases. The HyperPod training operator checks the logs of each HyperPodPyTorchJob against rules in the job specification and restarts the job when it hangs. The same rules can also restart a job whose throughput drops or whose loss spikes. You don’t need Ray for this. For Ray Train jobs, HyperPod hung job detection for Ray watches every worker by default, with no changes to your code.

It has been revealed that create a rules file on shared storage. The smallest valid file turns on default detection:.

The agent uses whatever rules file a job points to and doesn’t check who owns it. Anyone who can edit the file, or replace it in its directory, can change detection for every job that uses it, including making the agent cancel those jobs. The chmod 600 in the example keeps a personal rules file private to its owner. For a file that a team shares, use chmod 644 so the team can read it and only its maintainer can edit it. In both cases, make the parent directory writable only by its owner so nobody can swap the file.

Then point the job at the rules file when you submit it:.

To use one rules file for many jobs, you can also set HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES in a shell profile or a site-wide profile script.

When a monitored job starts, the first lines of its output show that the agent registered it:.

These lines also appear when the rules file is invalid, so check CloudWatch for a CONFIG_ERROR event too, as described in the next section.

Industry observers note that default detection can’t catch a job that keeps its GPUs busy without making progress, so we recommend at least one rule that watches for your training steps or epochs. The following rules file cancels the job if no epoch finishes for 45 minutes, or as soon as an NCCL error appears:.

By default, the agent reads the job’s Slurm output file. To watch a different file, set monitoring.log_file. To cut false positives, set metric_evaluation_data_points on a rule so that several 10-second checks in a row must fail before the agent declares a hang. A rules file can have up to 20 rules and be up to 1 MB.

Start with "action": "notify" while you tune timeouts and patterns, and switch to cancel once the events match real hangs.

Sources indicate that hyperPod writes detection events from the controller node to the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters//, in the stream SageMakerHangJobDetectionEvents//. Events for every job land in this stream, whichever node the job ran on. To find the events for one job, filter by its job ID:.

We tested each detection method on a HyperPod Slurm cluster with two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. The first test job allocated GPU memory and then stopped producing output. Default detection flagged it 15 minutes after its last output:.

The layer field demonstrates which method fired: signal_evaluator for default detection, or pattern_evaluator for a custom rule. In a second test, a progress rule with a 2-minute timeout fired 2 minutes after the job’s last step. In a third, an error rule fired about one second after the job printed an NCCL error line. Because that rules file used cancel, the agent also wrote a HANG_ACTION_TAKEN event with the action Slurm took (we’ve left out the time, level, and msg fields):.

Industry observers note that slurm put the job back in the queue, and the requeued run started about 2.5 minutes later. sacct indicates both runs:.

Slurm requeues a job up to the cluster’s MaxBatchRequeue limit, which was 5 on our cluster. A job submitted with #SBATCH --no-requeue reported "action": "cancel" instead and stayed canceled. With notify, there’s no HANG_ACTION_TAKEN event. The agent follows HANG_DETECTED with a record that says Hang notification sent, no automatic action taken.

If a rules file is missing or invalid, the agent doesn’t monitor the job and writes a CONFIG_ERROR event instead. Here’s the event for a rules file with a JSON syntax error:.

Recent findings suggest that the job ran to completion without monitoring, and nothing appeared in sbatch, squeue, or the job’s output. Test a new rules file with a short job and check for this event before you use it for production jobs.

It has been revealed that with notify, the job keeps running until someone acts on the event. To get an alert, create a CloudWatch metric filter for HANG_DETECTED events and an alarm that notifies an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic:.

To turn off detection for a job that would otherwise inherit HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES, add --no-hang-detection to srun, or to sbatch to cover every step in the job. To turn it off for every job that uses a rules file, set "enabled": false in the file. Running jobs keep their current settings, and the change applies to jobs you submit afterward.

Sources indicate that node health is essential to reliable distributed training, but it does not provide a complete picture of workload health. MultiNodeTrainingValidation detects instances that pass hardware diagnostics but produce invalid training results. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent connects Kubernetes infrastructure failures to the jobs, pods, and nodes involved. Hung job detection identifies Slurm jobs that remain active after they stop making progress and can return them to the queue automatically.

In a recent development, together, these capabilities help you detect failures earlier, shorten investigations, and raise goodput by reducing the GPU time spent on workloads that can’t make useful progress. Use MultiNodeTrainingValidation when adding or revalidating capacity, run the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent continuously on supported Amazon EKS clusters, and begin hung job detection in notify mode before you switch to automatic cancellation. To get started, see the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency documentation for Amazon EKS and the hung job detection documentation for Slurm. To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page.

Breaking: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • It has been revealed that the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
  • According to recent reports, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

It has been revealed that the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

According to recent reports, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

In a recent development, the model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

Recent findings suggest that radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

Recent findings suggest that 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Industry observers note that stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Industry observers note that our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

It has been revealed that cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

Industry observers note that we’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

Recent findings suggest that we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

This could allow an attacker that is able to pass a crafted message definition file to the user to inject arbitrary code into the generated program. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, CISA has added four upcoming vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not right now listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.15507v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) plays a crucial role in tackling complex tasks, yet its reliance on deep neural networks makes the learned policies opaque. To enhance the trustworthiness of RL policies, existing work (e.g., the SILVER framework [Li et al., 2025]) has focused on Shapley-based interpretability, but is typically restricted to low-dimensional state spaces, binary-action settings, and a single class of linear surrogate. We propose ReShap, a policy-distillation framework that extends Shapley-based interpretability to high-dimensional, multi-action environments. ReShap extracts compact feature representations from raw image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution to characterize how each feature contributes to the policy's decisions, and distills the deep RL policy into an interpretable surrogate trained on the full set of (state, policy-action) pairs along the policy's visited distribution. We instantiate the surrogate with three interpretable model families (decision trees, linear regression, and logistic regression) and compare their fidelity and task return. We evaluate ReShap on Atari and Box2D environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct a human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the resulting policies. Results show that ReShap preserves competitive task performance, that decision trees generally outperform linear and logistic regression, and that linear regression is weakest in most settings.

arXiv:2611.14912v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.

Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b).
